newsitem.title: USA: Speedy advice on the Internet.
newsitem.headline: Speedy advice on the Internet.

text.p: The heavy volume of business travel done by car makes speeding tickets an occupational hazard for some.
That may help account for a good part of the popularity of an Internet site that purports to blow the whistle on speed traps, one that is being accessed by as many as 40,000 people in some weeks.
The site -- www.telalink.net/speedtrap/ -- details speed traps in the United States, Canada and 18 other countries. The biggest volume of information appears to be from the United States.
It is specific -- right down to the cornfield at the edge of town where the unsuspecting driver doesn't realize the 35 m.p.h. speed zone is still in effect.

Andrew Warner who put the site together is a student on the verge of graduating from Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tenn. So far, he says, no real competitors have emerged since he jumped into the field in 1995.
"There are a few knockoffs but nothing close," he said. "I have more than 13,000 traps. I don't know of anybody that has really stuck with it, though a few have made nice starts."

Most of the information comes from travelers who report traps to the site. The process is self-correcting, Warner says, because someone else coming down the same road later on will often verify the same information or, if necessary, straighten out misinformation.
In addition, Warner says, he has become adept at spotting entries that don't ring true. The advertising on the pages, he adds, helps pay for expenses but little else.
Warner is not advocating speeding -- even these days when many states have upped their limits to 75 m.p.h. and Montana has abolished daytime limits completely.
"I get quite a bit of feedback" from law enforcement agencies, he said.
"The larger departments love it for the most part. It makes their job easier. Many of them view traffic duty as a lesser job," he said.
Some small-town police departments are not as thrilled, he said, since some classic speed traps operated as revenue producers could be unmasked.
"I certainly sympathize with them and there are some serious funding issues, but that still doesn't make it right," he said.

Many of the speed traps are pinpointed by longitude and latitude, placing them within a square mile of where they are. With technology such as global satellite positioning that is already becoming available for on-the-road use, it may soon be possible to offer drivers a service that would set off an alarm in the car when approaching any of the speed traps identified on the site along a given route, he said.

Notice of the speed trap site comes from Promos Hotel Corp., the chain that includes Embassy Suites, Hampton Inn and Homewood Suites hotels. It was among several sites the company recently listed as useful for travel planners.

Those who do decide slow down might want to dial up another of the sites it recommended, for diversion. At http://ourworld.compuserve.com/homepages/martince/ can be found the world's largest roadside attractions.
In alphabetical order, some with pictures, are listed such draws as the world's largest thermometer (in Baker, Calif.) and the world's largest lutefisk, a Norwegian dish (in Madison, Minn.).
